lessonTitle: The Strain-Life Approach and Low-Cycle Fatigue

blocks.text: The turbine casing of a jet engine is heated and cooled on every flight. It never carries a large mechanical load, but the constrained thermal expansion forces the metal at its hottest spot past yield, cycle after cycle. The life is a few thousand flights, and no stress-life curve built from elastic stress can describe it.

blocks.markdown: When cyclic loading is high enough to cause significant **plastic** deformation each cycle, stress is a poor measure because it changes little while strain changes a lot. The **strain-life approach** therefore uses the strain amplitude $\Delta\varepsilon/2$ as the controlling variable. In the stable cyclic response, a stress-strain hysteresis loop forms, and its total strain width splits into an elastic part, recovered on unloading, and a plastic part, the loop's width at zero stress.

blocks.caption: Total strain amplitude is the sum of elastic and plastic amplitudes; the elastic part follows from the stress amplitude $\sigma_a$ and Young's modulus $E$.

blocks.title: Reversals and cycles
blocks.text: One cycle contains two reversals. Strain-life equations are written in $2N$, the number of reversals to failure, so $N$ is cycles to failure.

blocks.markdown: Each component has its own power-law life relation. The elastic part is Basquin's relation in strain form, and the plastic part is the **Coffin-Manson** relation. Adding them gives the strain-life equation.

blocks.caption: Strain-life equation. $\sigma_f'$ = fatigue strength coefficient (MPa), $b$ = fatigue strength exponent (about $-0.05$ to $-0.12$), $\varepsilon_f'$ = fatigue ductility coefficient, $c$ = fatigue ductility exponent (about $-0.5$ to $-0.7$).

blocks.title: Splitting the strain amplitude at a given life
blocks.prompt: A steel (assumed typical constants) has $\sigma_f'=1000$ MPa, $E=200$ GPa, $b=-0.09$, $\varepsilon_f'=0.5$, $c=-0.6$. Find the elastic, plastic and total strain amplitude at $N=10^{4}$ cycles.
blocks.answer: Elastic 0.00205, plastic 0.00131, total 0.00336 (about 39 percent of the total is plastic).

blocks.caption: The plastic and elastic lines cross at the transition life.

blocks.title: Life at a given strain amplitude
blocks.prompt: For the same steel, find the number of cycles at which the total strain amplitude is $\Delta\varepsilon/2 = 0.005$.

steps.text: The equation cannot be solved algebraically for $N$, so iterate: try $2N=2000$.
That is greater than 0.005, so the life is longer. Refine with a numerical search (bisection) until the sum equals 0.005.
Convert reversals to cycles and check by substitution (total amplitude $=0.005$).

blocks.answer: About 2983 cycles; this lies in the low-cycle regime, and the plastic term is dominant.

blocks.markdown: The two lines cross at the **transition life**, where elastic and plastic amplitudes are equal. Setting $\frac{\sigma_f'}{E}(2N_t)^b=\varepsilon_f'(2N_t)^c$ gives $2N_t=(\varepsilon_f'E/\sigma_f')^{1/(b-c)}$. For the steel above, $2N_t\approx8348$ reversals, or about 4174 cycles. Below it the plastic strain controls; above it the elastic strain does.

items: **Prefer strain-life** for low-cycle fatigue (lives below about $10^{4}$ cycles), thermal fatigue, and cases with notches where the root yields locally while the bulk is elastic.
**Prefer strain-life** when load sequence or plasticity matters, because strain-life tracks local strain history and mean-stress relaxation.
**Stress-life is adequate** for high-cycle fatigue, where strains are almost fully elastic and stress is a good measure of damage.

blocks.title: Choose by the plastic strain
blocks.text: If the plastic strain amplitude is small compared with the elastic part, the S-N approach is simpler and accurate. If the plastic part is significant (life near or below the transition life), use strain-life.

points: Total strain amplitude is the sum of elastic ($\sigma_a/E$) and plastic parts.
$\Delta\varepsilon/2=(\sigma_f'/E)(2N)^b+\varepsilon_f'(2N)^c$ - Basquin elastic term plus Coffin-Manson plastic term; solve for life by iteration.
Strain-life is preferred for low-cycle, thermal and notch-root fatigue; stress-life suits high-cycle elastic loading.

questions.stem: In strain-life analysis, how is the total strain amplitude related to its components?

options.text: It equals the plastic amplitude only
It equals the elastic amplitude only
It is the product of the elastic and plastic amplitudes
It is the sum of the elastic and plastic strain amplitudes

questions.correctOptionText: It is the sum of the elastic and plastic strain amplitudes

distractorRationale.c: Strains add; they are not multiplied.

questions.explanation: A hysteresis loop has a recoverable elastic width $\sigma_a/E$ and a plastic width. Adding the two gives the total strain amplitude that enters the strain-life equation.

questions.stem: For which situation is a strain-life method most appropriate?

options.text: A shaft with a purely elastic stress and a life of $10^{8}$ cycles
A static tensile loading
A creep test at constant stress
A component with significant plasticity each cycle and a life of a few thousand cycles

questions.correctOptionText: A component with significant plasticity each cycle and a life of a few thousand cycles

distractorRationale.a: That is a high-cycle elastic case suited to S-N.
distractorRationale.b: There is no cycling in static loading.

questions.explanation: When plastic strain accumulates each cycle, strain amplitude is the controlling variable and stress is nearly constant. This is the regime of low-cycle fatigue, where strain-life is the appropriate method.

questions.stem: In the strain-life equation, which term dominates at very long lives?

options.text: The elastic (Basquin) term, because its exponent $b$ is much shallower than $c$
The plastic term, because its exponent is shallower
Neither, both are zero
The plastic term, because plastic strains are always larger

questions.correctOptionText: The elastic (Basquin) term, because its exponent $b$ is much shallower than $c$

distractorRationale.a: Correct: with the shallower slope $b$ the elastic term decays slowly and exceeds the plastic term.
distractorRationale.b: The plastic term decays faster, since $|c|>|b|$.
distractorRationale.d: Plastic strain falls off quickly with life.

questions.explanation: Because $|c|>|b|$, the plastic term falls more quickly with increasing $N$ than the elastic term. Beyond the transition life the elastic term is the larger and the response is nearly elastic.

questions.stem: A notched component is loaded by a nominal stress that is elastic, but the notch root yields locally. Why is strain-life a better choice than a nominal stress-life approach?

options.text: Nominal stress is always larger than local stress
The notch has no effect on fatigue
Local strain at the root, not nominal stress, controls the damage and is captured by the strain-life method
Strain-life ignores plasticity

questions.correctOptionText: Local strain at the root, not nominal stress, controls the damage and is captured by the strain-life method

distractorRationale.a: The local stress is higher than nominal at a notch.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: it uses the local strain.

questions.explanation: The local strain at the notch root includes plastic deformation even though the bulk is elastic. The strain-life method uses this local strain amplitude, whereas the nominal stress is a misleading measure.

questions.stem: Two steels have the same strength coefficient $\sigma_f'$ but steel B has a higher ductility coefficient $\varepsilon_f'$. How do their strain-life curves differ?

options.text: Steel B has a shorter life everywhere
Steel B has a longer life only at very long lives
There is no difference
Steel B has a longer low-cycle life, with little difference at very long lives

questions.correctOptionText: Steel B has a longer low-cycle life, with little difference at very long lives

distractorRationale.a: A higher ductility coefficient raises the plastic term and the life.
distractorRationale.b: The elastic term (long life) depends on $\sigma_f'$ which is unchanged.

questions.explanation: The ductility coefficient scales the plastic term, which dominates short lives, so B performs better in low-cycle fatigue. The elastic term, which controls long lives, is unchanged because $\sigma_f'$ is the same.

questions.stem: A fatigue specimen has stress amplitude $\sigma_a=300$ MPa and $E=205$ GPa. Find the elastic strain amplitude in microstrain ($10^{-6}$).
questions.explanation: $\varepsilon_{ea}=\sigma_a/E=300/205000=0.001463$, which is 1463 microstrain. Stress and modulus must be in the same unit (MPa).

questions.stem: In a strain-controlled test the total strain amplitude is 0.0040 and the stress amplitude is 500 MPa; $E=200$ GPa. Find the plastic strain amplitude in microstrain.
questions.explanation: The elastic amplitude is $500/200000=0.0025$, so the plastic amplitude is $0.0040-0.0025=0.0015$, i.e. 1500 microstrain. The plastic part is about 37 percent of the total.

questions.stem: In a low-cycle test the plastic strain amplitude is 0.010. For a material with $\varepsilon_f'=0.35$ and $c=-0.58$ (assumed), use the Coffin-Manson relation $\Delta\varepsilon_p/2=\varepsilon_f'(2N)^c$ to estimate the number of cycles $N$ to failure.
questions.explanation: Solving, $2N=(0.010/0.35)^{1/(-0.58)}=(0.02857)^{-1.724}=459.4$ reversals, so $N=230$ cycles. Converting reversals to cycles requires dividing by two.

questions.stem: Give three situations in which a strain-life approach is preferable to a stress-life approach, and explain the physical reason in each case.
markingGuide: Low-cycle fatigue, where plastic strain is significant and stress hardly changes with life
Notch roots that yield locally, so local strain, not nominal stress, drives damage
Thermal fatigue or constrained expansion, where strain is imposed
Mentions that strain-life can include plastic strain and mean-stress relaxation, while stress-life is adequate for elastic high-cycle loading
questions.explanation: The strain-life method captures plastic damage and local yielding, which stress-life cannot. For purely elastic high-cycle loading the two methods agree and the simpler stress-life approach is adequate.

questions.stem: A steel has $\sigma_f'=900$ MPa, $E=200$ GPa, $b=-0.1$, $\varepsilon_f'=0.4$, $c=-0.55$ (assumed). (a) Compute the elastic and plastic strain amplitudes at $N=10^{4}$ cycles. (b) A component is cycled at a total strain amplitude of 0.0030. Decide whether it will survive $10^{4}$ cycles, and state the predicted life.
markingGuide: Total at $N=10^{4}$ is 0.0034, above 0.0030, so the life at 0.0030 exceeds $10^{4}$ cycles
Gives life from iteration of about 1.47\times10^{4} cycles
Direction check: a smaller strain amplitude gives a longer life
questions.explanation: At $N=10^{4}$ the strain-life equation gives a total amplitude of 0.0034. Since 0.0030 is lower than this, the component lasts longer than $10^{4}$ cycles. Iterating gives about 1.47\times10^{4} cycles.
